title: U.S. Senate · Maine

context.text: Graham Platner won the June 9, 2026 Democratic ranked-choice primary (72.1% in round 1) but withdrew from the race. A Democratic convention was held July 25, 2026 to fill the vacancy; Troy Dale Jackson won that convention and appears on the general-election ballot as the Democratic nominee.
Susan Collins won the Republican primary unopposed after other candidates withdrew.

Several other candidates are certified write-in candidates for the general election: Sigrid Ann Olson (D), Ashley Webb (D), Joseph Steinberger (Faith in Humanity Party), Brent Andrews (Unaffiliated), Michael Turcotte (Unenrolled), and Gina Oswald (Independent). None of these appear pre-printed on the ballot; voters must write in their names.

priorities.text: Campaigned on her experience and seniority in the Senate, citing her role as Chairman of the Senate Appropriations Committee.
priorities.quote: As Chairman of the Senate Appropriations Committee, Susan has secured millions of dollars in federal investments for workforce development and training programs.

positions.summary: In December 2025 Collins joined Sen. Moreno in introducing the CARE Act, which extends the enhanced ACA premium tax credits for two years while adding an income cap and a $25 minimum monthly premium.
positions.quote: extending the Affordable Care Act enhanced premium tax credits for two years and putting a reasonable income cap on these subsidies

positions.summary: In 2022 Collins and Sen. Murkowski introduced the Reproductive Choice Act to codify the abortion rights established by Roe v. Wade and Planned Parenthood v. Casey; Collins said she supports those rights.
positions.quote: I support the abortion rights established by Roe v. Wade and affirmed by Planned Parenthood v. Casey.

positions.summary: Collins cosponsored the Trade Review Act of 2025, which would end new tariffs after 60 days unless Congress approves them, and said tariffs on Canada often harm Maine's economy and consumers.
positions.quote: these tariffs often harm Maine's economy and consumers

positions.summary: In an April 2026 statement on her vote for a resolution directing removal of U.S. forces from hostilities against Iran, Collins said the Constitution gives Congress an essential role in decisions of war and peace.
positions.quote: The Constitution gives Congress an essential role in decisions of war and peace

record.text: Author of the Social Security Fairness Act, which was signed into law in 2025.
Serves as Chairman of the Senate Appropriations Committee.

candidates.name: Troy Dale Jackson
candidates.ballotNote: Won the July 25, 2026 Democratic convention held to fill the nomination after Graham Platner's withdrawal.

priorities.text: Campaigns on an economic-populist message centered on his working-class background.
priorities.quote: I've spent my life fighting that same rigged system—from the logging woods to the Maine Senate. I'm running to carry forward Maine's working-class movement, defeat Susan Collins and give people a senator who will fight like hell for them—not the wealthy and well-connected.

positions.summary: Jackson's campaign priorities page lists passing Medicare for all.
Jackson's campaign priorities page lists dismantling and abolishing ICE.

As Maine Senate President, voted yes on final enactment of LD 2224, which expanded background-check requirements for private gun sales and revised the state's "yellow flag" law after the October 2023 Lewiston mass shooting; the Senate passed it 18-15 on April 17, 2024.
Jackson's campaign priorities page lists taxing billionaires and making corporations pay their fair share.
Jackson's campaign priorities page lists passing a federal right to abortion.
positions.quote: Pass a federal right to abortion.

positions.summary: Jackson's campaign priorities page says no U.S. tax dollars should go to Israel's military.
positions.quote: No U.S. tax dollars to Israel's military.

record.text: Served as Democratic leader and Senate President during his tenure in the Maine Senate (2008-2014, 2016-2024).
Voted yes on LD 2224 (expanding background-check requirements for private gun sales and revising the state's "yellow flag" law), which passed the Senate 18-15 on April 17, 2024.
Voted yes on LD 1964 (establishing a state paid family and medical leave program funded by a payroll tax), which the Senate advanced 22-12 on June 21, 2023.

candidates.name: Ashley Webb
candidates.ballotNote: Certified write-in candidate; not pre-printed on the general-election ballot.

priorities.text: Prioritizes healthcare reform focused on patients, drawing on her experience as a patient advocate.
priorities.quote: I've spent years navigating a healthcare system that too often protects itself before it protects the people it serves, and I'll bring that firsthand knowledge to fighting for reimbursement and staffing models that give clinicians real time with patients.

priorities.text: Proposes a new highway corridor connecting Farmington and Skowhegan to the interstate system to address rural infrastructure gaps in Franklin and Somerset counties.

positions.summary: Her campaign website describes a proposed Women's Health Earned Income Credit funded by closing tax loopholes for high-net-worth individuals and raising billionaire tax rates.
positions.quote: funded entirely by closing high-net-worth tax loopholes and spiking billionaire tax rates

candidates.researchNotes: Write-in candidate; positions drawn from her Ballotpedia Candidate Connection survey and the Mission Statement page of her campaign website (truthpointusa.com). Her survey and 'My Platform' page cover healthcare accountability, rural infrastructure and foreign policy in terms that do not squarely answer the guide's other issue statements, so no other stances or statements were added.

researchNotes: Key floor votes and FEC totals for incumbent Susan Collins are added later by script. Six candidates are certified write-ins with little to no independently verifiable public record within the research budget for this race; they are included for completeness since Ballotpedia lists them as running in the general election, but most entries are minimal. Biography gaps: the six write-in candidates have no public biography beyond party and town of residence (Spectrum News, Aug. 26, 2026) and, for Ashley Webb, her Ballotpedia survey; Ballotpedia has no pages for Brent Andrews or Michael Turcotte (disambiguation only).
